items.notes: Broken links (X): every *_COG.TIF link on the PGDA illumination page (e.g. https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/MoonIllumination/AVGVISIB_85S_060M_201608_COG.TIF, ..._EARTH_COG.TIF, AVGVISIB_65S_240M_201608_COG.TIF, LPSR_85S_060M_201608_COG.TIF, SKYV_65S_240M_COG.TIF) returned a PGDA "404 – Not Found" HTML page (served with HTTP status 200, 3,789 bytes) on 2026-11-14. The non-COG .TIF works. Also, on that page the "JP2" link for LPSR 65S points to the .IMG, and three north "IMG" links point to .JP2. Method summary (quoted): "Mazarico et al. (2011) used 240 meters-per-pixel polar maps from LOLA and computed the illumination conditions at the lunar poles over an entire lunar nutation cycle (~18.6 years) with a timestep of one hour"; products are "typically averages over long time periods"; "polar stereographic projection, with a reference radius of 1737.4 km and true scale at the pole"; "PDS IMG format (int16 binary tables) and the GeoJPEG2000 format". PGDA note: "Contact us if you have specific needs (e.g., a given duration for a given site)". On GeoTIFF/COG conversions: "Scaling/offets should be applied automatically for the GeoTIFFs, but please refer to the PDS label files"; "values seen when zoomed out may be taken from overview layers, which are built by averaging true full-resolution values. Be aware of this if doing quantitative analysis." README: maps "extend to +/- 770 km or +/- 151 km"; "Some maps show linear artifacts that arise from the topographic DEMS". ODE catalogues the same family as LRO/LOLA product types GDRVIS (48 products), GDRPSR (28), GDRSKY (12).

Artemis III 2022 candidate regions (13) — NASA Trek feature service A3_Named_regions_SP
items.variable: 13 square region polygons; fields FID, label, selected
items.coverage: 13 regions, each "within six degrees of latitude of the lunar South Pole"
items.format: ArcGIS feature service (JSON); CRS PROJCS["Moon2000_spole" ... SPHEROID["Moon_2000_IAU_IAG",1737400.0,0.0] ... PROJECTION["Stereographic_South_Pole"] ... central_meridian 0, standard_parallel_1 -90, metres]
items.notes: Query used returned ACAO *. Polygon extents are quoted from the service (x, y in metres, south polar stereographic). Centre lat/lon were computed in the research session from the polygon centre with the spherical polar stereographic inverse (lat = −90 + 2·atan(rho/(2R)), lon = atan2(x, y), R = 1,737,400 m), i.e. they are derived values, not NASA-published numbers. centre_lon_deg_360 is the same derived longitude expressed in 0..360 (lon+360 for negative values). NASA description attached to the layer: the 13 regions were "announced by NASA on August 19 2022"; "Each of these regions is located within six degrees of latitude of the lunar South Pole"; evaluated "using criteria including terrain slope, ease of communications with Earth, and lighting conditions"; "All 13 regions contain sites that provide continuous access to sunlight throughout a 6.5-day period – the planned duration of the Artemis III surface mission"; goal "to land close enough to a permanently shadowed region to allow crew to conduct a moonwalk". 2022 release page https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-identifies-candidate-regions-for-landing-next-americans-on-moon/ (URL returned 200; text not re-read). Note inference: the polygons are axis-aligned squares of 16, 20, 21 or 29.8 km side in stereographic x/y, i.e. schematic region boxes rather than surveyed boundaries; suitable as app 'regions of interest' but not as landing ellipses.
items.caveat: centre lat/lon derived by researcher (computed from Trek polygon centre), not NASA-published; no official polygon layer for the nine regions announced 2024-10-28 was found

Example output header: "Target body name: Sun (10) {source: DE441}; Center body name: Moon (301); Center geodetic: 0.0, -89.5, 0.0 {E-lon(deg),Lat(deg),Alt(km)}; Center pole/equ: MEAN_ME (high precision); Center radii: 1737.4, 1737.4, 1737.4 km; Vis. interferer: EARTH; Atmos refraction: NO (AIRLESS)". Quantity 4 definition (quoted): "Airless apparent azimuth and elevation of target center. Compensated for light-time, the gravitational deflection of light, stellar aberration, precession and nutation. Azimuth is measured clockwise from north ... Elevation angle is with respect to a plane perpendicular to the reference surface local zenith direction." Solar-presence flag * means "solar upper-limb on or above apparent horizon" of the reference sphere. Note inference: Horizons gives Sun/Earth elevation relative to the reference sphere only; terrain masking must be added from a DEM-derived horizon; its MEAN_ME site frame matches the ME frame of the LOLA products. algorithms.name: Horizon/illumination method (Mazarico et al. 2011)
algorithms.description: 240 m/px LOLA polar maps; illumination "over an entire lunar nutation cycle (~18.6 years) with a timestep of one hour"; light source treated as "a finite disc", so the same code gives Earth visibility by changing source position and size; sky visibility = "solid angle not obscured by topography". Products are "typically averages over long time periods". Earth visibility: "the Earth is considered visible if any part of its disc is not obscured, so it may be very slightly optimistic for radio link studies that would involve only DSN stations".
algorithms.caveat: Details of the Mazarico et al. 2011 implementation (number of azimuths, horizon range, treatment of the solar limb) were not verified from the paper itself

algorithms.name: LROC PSR identification from horizon elevation
algorithms.description: "the horizon elevation was determined in several directions based on polar DTMs" (60 m/px for 82–90°S, 120 m/px for 81–82°S); "digitization of south pole PSRs (larger than 5 square km)".

algorithms.name: Uncertainty propagation with statistical clones (Barker et al. 2021)
algorithms.description: Instead of the "infeasible computation of the full error-covariance matrix of the LDEM", "use the fractal nature of lunar topography to build a more computationally manageable statistical ensemble of clones with similar error properties as the data" (100 clones per site) to study "height and slope uncertainty, as well as the uncertainty in illumination conditions"; illumination evaluated at 1 m and 5 m above the surface, Jan 1 2024–Jan 1 2026.

parameters.observer_heights: 1 m and 5 m above the surface

algorithms.name: Empirical illumination from WAC images (Speyerer & Robinson 2013)
algorithms.description: Binary lit/unlit classification of 3,807 WAC images over one year, ratio lit/observed per 100 m pixel; time-weighted variant interpolates gaps (gaps linearly interpolated; sparse periods weighted x2). "WAC images (n=3807) acquired over one lunar year from 15 February 2010 to 5 February 2011"; "Temporal gaps were filled with 229 observations"; "map-projected at 100 meters/pixel in polar stereographic projection onto a 30 m LOLA DEM"; repeat imaging "approximately every 2 hours".

algorithms.name: Rendered illumination simulation (NASA SVS 4930/5027)
algorithms.description: LOLA terrain lit for every 2 h step, 35,064 frames for 2023–2030 (5027: 17,532 time steps for 2025–2028).

algorithms.name: Roughness definitions used by GSFC (Barker et al. 2023)
algorithms.description: Plane-fit residual spread ("spread of height residuals of individual LOLA spots around a plane fit to the LDEM within a circular window whose diameter is equal to a baseline"), plane-fit slope ("corresponding slope (in degrees) of the plane fit"), and RMS height deviation ("RMS height deviation (in meters) between a central point and surrounding annulus") at baselines 100/200/400/800/1600 m.

algorithms.name: Shape-from-Shading (photoclinometry) with Ames Stereo Pipeline
algorithms.description: PGDA pipelines use ASP + ISIS + GDAL; image selection keeps "at least three distinct illumination directions per pixel"; 30 m/px tiles of 10 km x 10 km with ~30 images each for the 60–80°S approach strip.

algorithms.name: ML super-resolution demo (Schroedinger Bridge, 320 m → 20 m/px)
algorithms.description: "RMS elevation error of 5-6 m" and "mean slope errors below 2°" on a 9,171-patch test set; trained on 91,708 patches from LOLA polar DEMs > 80° latitude rendered "with a ray-tracing planetary shape-model renderer".

algorithms.name: Spherical polar stereographic inverse (south pole) used for Trek region centres
algorithms.description: lat = −90 + 2·atan(rho/(2R)), lon = atan2(x, y), R = 1,737,400 m (rho = distance of (x, y) from the pole). The LOLA south-pole stereographic convention places +y toward longitude 0° and +x toward 90°E (verified numerically in the session: the Trek "Malapert Massif" box at x ≈ 0, y ≈ +121 km maps to lon ≈ 0°, and "Faustini Rim A" at x = +64 km, y = 0 maps to lon 90°E with the standard inverse).
algorithms.evidence: computed in the research session (derived by researcher)

algorithms.name: LOLA PDS3 IMG DN to height/radius
algorithms.description: 16-bit LSB signed integers, height (m) = DN x 0.5, radius = DN x 0.5 + 1,737,400; "pixel registration"; projection offsets 15167.5 for a 30336-pixel grid at 5 m; frame "MEAN EARTH/POLAR AXIS OF DE421"; planetocentric latitude, east-positive longitude. Float IMG versions store metres directly at twice the byte size. Pixels per side derived = sqrt(bytes/2).

algorithms.name: Geotransform for ldem_875s_5m
algorithms.description: Upper-left corner x = −75,840 m, y = +75,840 m, pixel 5 m (derived from LINE/SAMPLE_PROJECTION_OFFSET 15167.5 and matching Trek's bbox).

algorithms.name: Diviner PCP table coordinates
algorithms.description: PCP tables give x, y as "Polar Stereographic X-Coordinate, normalized by the mean lunar radius 1737.4 km" with UNKNOWN_CONSTANT −9999, INVALID_CONSTANT −9998; the tables are point lists that must be gridded (multiply by 1737.4 km).
algorithms.evidence: PDS format file; gridding step is a note inference

algorithms.name: MOON_ME vs MOON_PA frame transformation
algorithms.description: "a constant coordinate transformation from MOON_PA to MOON_ME ... results in an offset of approximately 875 m"; rotation angle "approximately 0.0288473 degrees" (moon_080317.tf, DE421); for DE421 TKFRAME_31007_ANGLES = ( 67.92 78.56 0.30 ) arcseconds, axes (3, 2, 1); SPICE recipe furnsh('moon_080317.tf'), furnsh('moon_assoc_me.tf'), PXFORM('MOON_ME','MOON_PA', et, …). DE440 frame kernel: separation ME–PA "approximately 0.02886 degrees ... approximately 875 m".
algorithms.evidence: PGDA 95 and NAIF frame kernel, quoted (two slightly different angle values kept with their sources)

algorithms.name: Sun/Earth azimuth-elevation at a lunar surface point via JPL Horizons
algorithms.description: EPHEM_TYPE=OBSERVER, CENTER='coord@301', COORD_TYPE=GEODETIC, SITE_COORD='E-lon deg, lat deg, alt km', COMMAND '10' (Sun) or '399' (Earth), QUANTITIES='4' ("Airless apparent azimuth and elevation of target center..."). Elevation is relative to the reference sphere only; terrain masking must be added from a DEM-derived horizon (note inference).

algorithms.name: NASA Trek pre-computed slope classes

algorithms.name: Minimal landing-window pipeline (note inference)
algorithms.description: (1) load DEM in polar stereographic ME frame; (2) for each candidate pixel (plus mast height h) precompute horizon elevation vs azimuth; (3) for each time step get Sun and Earth direction in MOON_ME via SpiceyPy (de440.bsp, moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc, moon_de440_250416.tf, naif0012.tls) or Horizons; convert to local azimuth/elevation; (4) compute visible fraction of the solar disc above the terrain horizon (Sun angular radius about 0.27°†) and Earth visibility (any part of disc, per Mazarico, or centre above horizon plus margin for DSN); (5) scan for intervals where illumination ≥ threshold continuously for the stay duration (NASA: 6.5 days in 2022 text; 5.75–6.25 days in the 2026 abstract) and Earth is visible; (6) repeat on DEM clones or with ±error rasters for confidence.

for each candidate pixel (plus mast height h) precompute horizon elevation vs azimuth
for each time step get Sun and Earth direction in MOON_ME via SpiceyPy (de440.bsp, moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc, moon_de440_250416.tf, naif0012.tls) or Horizons; convert to local azimuth/elevation

compute visible fraction of the solar disc above the terrain horizon (Sun angular radius about 0.27°†) and Earth visibility (any part of disc, per Mazarico, or centre above horizon plus margin for DSN)
scan for intervals where illumination ≥ threshold continuously for the stay duration (NASA: 6.5 days in 2022 text; 5.75–6.25 days in the 2026 abstract) and Earth is visible
repeat on DEM clones or with ±error rasters for confidence

algorithms.name: Cost of horizon precomputation and time stepping (note inference †)
algorithms.description: Horizon precomputation scales as N_pixels x N_azimuths x search radius (far-field terrain up to ~150+ km matters at grazing Sun because of lunar curvature); time stepping is then O(N_pixels) per step. 18.6 years hourly = about 163,000 steps (18.6 x 8,766 h). A 5 m site grid of 4,000 x 4,000 pixels with 720 azimuths needs multi-resolution horizons (fine DEM near field, 60–240 m DEM far field) or GPU/Embree ray tracing.
algorithms.evidence: Inference marked † (background knowledge not verified against a source in this session)
algorithms.caveat: no source URL in notes (researcher inference, not verified)

algorithms.name: Slope/roughness from DEM (note inference †)
algorithms.description: Slope via finite differences (Horn) at a stated baseline; roughness as RMS deviation from a fitted plane or as terrain ruggedness (the PGDA SfS product ships "VRM roughness maps at multiple baselines"); use PGDA LDSM_* and LDRM_* rasters directly where the baseline fits, and report slope together with *_slperr. Because ~90% of 5 m pixels are interpolated, sub-20 m slope from LOLA alone is not a measurement.
algorithms.evidence: Inference marked † (background knowledge not verified against a source in this session)

algorithms.name: Multi-criteria scoring (note inference)
algorithms.description: NASA gives criteria but no weights; an app must choose its own (hard constraints: slope below a limit over the ellipse, continuous sunlight for the stay, Earth visibility; soft scores: mean illumination, distance to PSR ≥ area threshold, ice-stability depth, Diviner max T, hazard density, DEM confidence/effective resolution). Any numeric weights should be labelled as the app's assumptions. No single NASA "water-ice favourability" raster was found; a composite must be built from Diviner max temperature / ice-stability depth, LAMP ratio, LOLA albedo, M3 detections, Mini-RF CPR and neutron WEH.

site_selection_statements.statement: NASA release dated Oct 28, 2024: "The refined candidate Artemis III lunar landing regions are, in no priority order: Peak near Cabeus B; Haworth; Malapert Massif; Mons Mouton Plateau; Mons Mouton; Nobile Rim 1; Nobile Rim 2; de Gerlache Rim 2; Slater Plain".
site_selection_statements.caveat: No official shapefile/GeoJSON/KML for the nine 2024 regions was found; NASA publishes only names and a figure. Note inference: five names carry over unchanged from the 2022 polygons (Haworth, Malapert Massif, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, de Gerlache Rim 2); "Mons Mouton" corresponds to the feature formerly called Leibnitz Beta; whether the 2024 boxes equal the 2022 boxes is not confirmed; polygons for Peak near Cabeus B, Mons Mouton Plateau and Slater Plain would have to be digitised from the NASA figure or approximated from LROC ROI mosaic footprints.

site_selection_statements.statement: NTRS extended abstract 20250011660 "Artemis III Site Selection Update: Downselection From Thirteen to Nine Candidate Regions" (T. George, M. A. Rubio, S. J. Lawrence, P. Curell; for LPSC 2026): "Surface stay duration varies approximately 5.75 to 6.25 days depending on mission epoch"; operations from NRHO impose "strong temporal and geometric constraints on surface access"; constraints "evaluated simultaneously on a calendar basis"; terrain safety "focused on minimizing the degree of slope variability within a landing ellipse"; hazards include "impact craters, block populations, and rough or highly variable terrain"; "If Artemis III employs a Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication architecture, regions with greater Earth visibility are preferred"; "south polar illumination conditions exhibiting strong seasonal variability and shifting approximately 2-3 weeks per year"; "individual regions typically provide limited viable opportunities when all constraints are simultaneously satisfied".

georeferencing_facts.fact: All south-polar NASA rasters share one projection (polar stereographic, lat_0 = −90, lon_0 = 0, k = 1, sphere R = 1,737,400 m) but differ in container (PDS3 IMG int16 with scale 0.5, float IMG, JP2, GeoTIFF/COG, ASCII tables), in CRS code naming (IAU2000:30120 in Trek is south polar stereographic, whereas IAU_2015:30120 is a sinusoidal CRS; the IAU_2015 south-polar code is 30135), and in vintage (pre- vs post-track-adjustment). Everything is in the Mean-Earth/Polar-Axis (ME) frame of DE421, about 875 m away from the Principal-Axis frame.
ESRI:103878 ("Moon_2000_South_Pole_Stereographic") = identical string to IAU_2015:30135; ESRI:103877 is "Moon_2000_North_Pole_Stereographic"
spatialreference.org URL path uses an underscore (/ref/iau_2015/30135/); /ref/iau/30135/ and /ref/iau-2015/30135/ return 404
Moon Trek identifies its projections as urn:ogc:def:crs:IAU2000::30120 (south pole), urn:ogc:def:crs:IAU2000::30118 (north pole) and urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::104903 (equirectangular)

USGS STAC south-polar Kaguya items carry WKT PROJCS["Moon (2015) - Sphere / Ocentric / South Polar" ... SPHEROID["Moon (2015) - Sphere",1737400,0 ...] ... PROJECTION["Polar_Stereographic"], latitude_of_origin −90, central_meridian 0, scale_factor 1 ... AUTHORITY["IAU","30135"]]

PGDA GeoTIFFs: "south polar stereographic X/Y coords in meters, MOON_ME reference frame of ephemeris DE421"; "X/Y coords follow the Generic Mapping Tools 'pixel-registered' convention (i.e., they are the centers of the pixels)". PGDA XYZI clouds: product 78 README says X, Y, Z "(in km)"; product 90 says X, Y "in meters".

Inference: with pyproj/GDAL (PROJ >= 8 ships the IAU_2015 authority, per the spatialreference.org build note "PROJ 9.9.0"), use IAU_2015:30135 or the explicit PROJ string; do not pass Trek's "30120" to a IAU_2015-aware library.

Inference: reading PDS3 IMG: GDAL's PDS driver reads the detached .lbl (open the .lbl), applying scale/offset metadata; rasterio users should apply scales/offsets or multiply DN by 0.5 themselves. This is standard GDAL behaviour but was not exercised in this session.

Inference: for ephemeris work, compute Sun/Earth vectors in MOON_ME (DE440 alias) so they line up with ME-frame maps; mixing PA-frame vectors with ME-frame DEMs introduces up to ~875 m of horizontal mis-registration (about 0.029°), which matters for grazing-incidence horizon tests.

Inference: illumination results are sensitive to observer height: Barker et al. 2021 report markedly different statistics at 1 m and 5 m above the surface, so an app should expose solar-array/antenna height as a parameter.

Inference: pixel dimensions computed from byte counts are consistent with the label for ldem_875s_5m (30336) and with Trek's bbox (−75840…75840 m), so the other derived dimensions in the table are likely correct but were not label-checked individually.

The SVS frame sets are the only NASA-published dated lighting time series; they are perspective/orthographic renders at 1920x1080 without georeferencing metadata, so they suit visual validation or UI playback rather than quantitative window computation. Cadence check: 4,380 frames/year x 2 h = 8,760 h, consistent with the stated two-hour interval.
Average-illumination rasters rank sites but cannot answer "is the Sun up during a given 6-day stay"; landing windows need a horizon-based time-series computation (section 7) using DEM + ephemeris.

The 2016 AVGVISIB products are derived from pre-adjustment LOLA DEMs at 60–240 m/px; at landing-site scale (tens of metres) local illumination can differ materially, which is why Barker et al. 2021 recomputed illumination on 5 m DEMs with clones.
For an app, the Trek 240 m Diviner seasonal rasters and ice-stability-depth rasters are the lowest-effort volatile/thermal inputs (small files, tile/image services with CORS).

A browser-only app can use Trek (tiles, ImageServer identify, feature queries), ODE REST, USGS STAC/S3 and the LROC file host directly; for PGDA COGs, PDS Geosciences/imbrium IMG files, NAIF kernels and Horizons it needs a backend proxy or self-hosted copies, because no CORS header was returned (range requests are supported, so COG partial reads work once proxied or re-hosted).

Storage planning: prefer 20 m (80–90°S) for regional screening, 5 m for the polar cap and candidate regions; avoid the 10 m 83°S set (about 37 GB) unless Malapert/Mons Mouton detail at 10 m is required (those lie at about 84–86°S, outside the 87°S mosaic but inside the 5 m per-site DEMs Site20/Site20v2/Site23/Site06/DM2 and the 2026 SfS SDEMs).
The wave of Space Apps 2026 repositories suggests an official NASA challenge on exactly this theme exists; its resource list (not retrieved) would be worth checking for NASA-endorsed datasets.
